worstFirst.title: gpg --decrypt
worstFirst.archetype: Text adventure / interactive fiction (parser, rooms, branching)

axisA.notes: core_mechanic(1): parser command loop (decrypt/verify/hint/status) advancing floor-by-floor is a genuine text-adventure spine, but two floors are dead ends so the 'rooms' don't chain. control_feel(1): typed commands feel right for the genre yet are brittle — exact-string only, no synonyms/abbrev, no command history. fail_restart(1): wrong answers just print an error with no state loss and 'restart' reloads — but Floors 4 (XOR) and 5 (RSA) are UNWINNABLE, so the game cannot be completed, the single biggest mechanics failure. difficulty_curve(1) reasonable Caesar->AES ramp; juice_feedback(1) decrypt scramble animation + SFX is nice.

axisB.notes: technical_accuracy(0): multiple hard crypto errors verified by computation — Floor 4 XOR ciphertext decrypts to garbage with key 0x69 (no single-byte key yields 'MARCUS SEES THE KEY'; floor is unbeatable); Floor 5 RSA d=3031 is correct but ciphertexts 2269/2371/3233 decrypt to 439/1106/2928 (out-of-ASCII garbage), never 'KEYSAFE' (also only 3 ciphertexts for a 7-char answer); Floor 2 substitution mapping decodes the ciphertext to 'ZICDMJ RMAE...' not the stated 'VICTOR KRANE SOLD THE VAULT'; Floor 3 Vigenere with keyword VAULT yields 'NZOGR HMCVE...' not 'ELENA FROST KNOWS MOLES'. skill_exercised(0): only Floor 1 Caesar truly computes the answer — Floors 2/3/6/7/8 just string-match the typed solution or a keyword/agent name (no decoding performed), so the player mostly types the answer rather than doing cryptanalysis. scenario_realism(1): spy-thriller framing and cipher-per-floor progression are thematically apt but the RSA/XOR/hash-collision treatments are hand-wavy. scaffolding(2): per-floor hints, status, and briefings are solid.

axisC.notes: visual_polish(2): cohesive CRT terminal — scanline overlay, radial vignette, amber(#eab308)/green(#00ff41) glow, classified-doc panels, ASCII banners. art_consistency(2): on-brand Key-house gold, monospace, no emoji (only Unicode check/cross glyphs on Floor 7, acceptable). animation_effects(2): typewriter reveal, decrypt-scramble decode animation, cursor blink. audio(0): WebAudio-only bleeps + tension drone — thin and non-diegetic; for a text-adventure this is genre-acceptable, scored low only against production-quality bar.

worstFirst.genreNote: Text-adventure / interactive-fiction archetype teaching cryptography — Axis-B-DOMINANT. Thin juice/audio is genre-appropriate and not penalized on Axis A/C; Axis C scored as clean/legible/on-brand (strong). Decisive axis is B; never a Unity candidate.

health.mobile: Playable-in-theory on touch (autofocus text input opens keyboard) but poor mobile UX: requires typing exact commands with no on-screen buttons/affordances; body overflow:hidden with a position:fixed bottom input bar risks being obscured by the mobile soft keyboard. Viewport meta present. Desktop-first.

worstFirst.verdict: Presentation matches its CRT-terminal text-adventure archetype well, but as a cryptography teacher it fails its skill reference — two floors (XOR, RSA) are mathematically unwinnable and most floors string-match the answer instead of decrypting; highest-value fix is regenerating the Floor 4/5 (and 2/3) ciphertexts so they actually decrypt to their solutions and gate progression, restoring a completable, skill-exercising game.

worstFirst.title: Git Bisect

axisA.notes: core_mechanic(1): presents commit log + find-the-bad-commit framing, but does NOT implement or enforce binary search — you can inspect any commit freely and win by directly Mark-Bad'ing the breaking commit; marking good never eliminates/collapses the range. control_feel(2): inspect/mark buttons are clear and responsive. juice_feedback(1): diff modal + red pulse on reveal, but no sound and no real bisect step animation. difficulty_curve(2): 8 rounds ramp 8->12->16 commits with rising optimal steps. fail_restart(1): wrong Mark-Bad scores 0 but game just continues; no true fail/restart loop.

axisB.notes: technical_accuracy(1): most bug diffs are realistic and well-chosen (SELCT typo, '=' vs '===' assignment, while<=+removed page++ infinite loop, cents/100/100, port 578, removed @media block), BUT Round 1's 'breaking' diff is a no-op — deletion and addition lines are byte-identical, so it shows no actual bug. Also misrepresents git bisect: real bisect AUTO-checks-out the midpoint and collapses the range on each good/bad mark; here the player free-selects any commit. scenario_realism(2): bug reports and commit metadata are plausible. skill_exercised(1): player reads diffs and clicks — nothing forces actual binary-search halving, so it exercises 'spot the buggy diff' more than 'bisect'. scaffolding(2): strong concept box explains bisect + O(log n) and optimal-step scoring.

axisC.notes: visual_polish(2): clean git-themed dark UI, GitHub-style green/red diff lines, monospace hashes, gradient headers. art_consistency(2): no emoji, on-brand Code-house green (#059669), consistent styling. animation_effects(1): hover transitions, ambient pulse, red reveal pulse — modest, no real transitions between bisect steps. audio(0): none.

worstFirst.genreNote: Binary-search puzzle / knowledge-check hybrid — Axis-B-dominant. Thin juice and absent audio are genre-appropriate and not heavily penalized; Axis C judged on legibility/polish/on-brand (clean). The core problem is Axis A/B: it does not actually implement the binary-search mechanic it teaches. Not a Unity candidate (puzzle/quiz-classification archetype).

worstFirst.verdict: A clean, well-scaffolded git-themed puzzle with mostly-accurate bug diffs, but it fails its own premise — it never enforces binary search (you can free-inspect and directly Mark-Bad the culprit), misrepresents how git bisect actually collapses the range, and Round 1's breaking diff is a no-op with identical add/delete lines.

worstFirst.archetype: Turn-based attack/defend strategy + classify-the-lure (NOT tower defense)

axisA.notes: Genuine turn-based strategy loop is present: attack phase (spend attack budget, weigh cost vs success rate, skip-to-conserve), defense phase (binary classify + shop upgrades that mechanically reduce attack success via counters/effectiveness), resource economy, and difficulty scaling by round. core_mechanic=2, control_feel=2, difficulty_curve=2 (attacks unlock by difficulty tier as rounds advance). GAPS: (1) juice_feedback=1 — only a pulse CSS keyframe and border glows; no sound, no meaningful transitions, static result screens. (2) fail_restart=1 — only 'Play Again' does location.reload(); no mid-game restart, and the two phases feel disjoint rather than an adversary genuinely responding to your moves (the AI 'adversary intel' panel is cosmetic, not a reacting opponent).

axisB.notes: technical_accuracy=2 — attack taxonomy (phishing/spear/whaling/vishing/smishing/tailgating/baiting/watering-hole/pretexting/multi-vector) and countermeasures (email filtering, SAT, MFA, escort policy, USB locks, SIEM, pentest, IR) are all real, correctly named, and sensibly mapped; lure examples (paypa1-verify typosquat, bit.ly urgency, CEO wire-fraud confidentiality) model correct red flags. scaffolding=2 (per-round educational notes + defense recommendations). CRITICAL DEFECT lowering skill_exercised=1 and scenario_realism=1: the classify-the-lure decision is decoupled from content — isLegitimate is set by Math.random()>0.7, but the displayed 'example' text is ALWAYS a malicious lure. The player cannot reason from evidence; correct classification is literally a coin-flip, which teaches the wrong lesson for a defense-training game. The player DOES exercise strategy/resource skills but not the actual lure-recognition skill the title promises.

CRITICAL DECOUPLING (lines 1417-1426): a CORRECTLY configured tower ignores its own subnet and fires at ANY packet where p.isThreat is true — it never calls isInSubnet for correct towers (only the misconfigured branch checks the subnet). So the configured CIDR is discarded during actual play; a /30 WAF set to 192.168.100.200/30 will still shoot 10.0.0.x threats. The skill is exercised once as a placement MCQ (recall/selection), then irrelevant to the tower-defense loop — the player does not actually DO subnet filtering, they answer a quiz then play generic TD. Minor: Wave 4 hint says '256-host /24' (a /24 = 256 addresses but 254 usable hosts).
